title: Layout First Principles — What a Layout Is Doing
content:
A layout does four jobs. Every layout decision serves one of them, and a layout that serves none is arrangement, not design.

1. ORDER — it tells the eye where to start and where to go next. Achieved through size, contrast, position, and isolation.
2. GROUPING — it tells the reader which things belong together. Achieved almost entirely through relative proximity, secondarily through enclosure and shared background.
3. RHYTHM — it makes the page navigable at a glance by repeating intervals, so the reader can predict where the next thing will be.
4. BREATHING — it gives the important thing enough emptiness around it to register as important. Isolation is the cheapest and strongest emphasis mechanism available.

THE ORDER OF DECISIONS, which most layouts get backwards:
1. What is the content, actually? Real content, real lengths, real quantities.
2. What is the priority order of that content, for this user, on this screen?
3. What is the structural system — grid, columns, gutters, margins, per breakpoint?
4. Where does each piece of content go in that system, at what size?
5. Only then: type sizes, colours, borders, shadows.

Working in reverse — starting from a visual reference and pouring content into it — produces layouts that break the first time real content arrives. The single most reliable predictor of a layout that will survive contact with production is whether it was designed from real content.

THE TEST OF A LAYOUT: cover it, uncover it for two seconds, cover it again. What do you remember, and in what order? That is what the layout communicated. If it does not match the intended priority, the layout is wrong regardless of how it looks.

title: Grid Systems — Choosing and Specifying One
content:
A grid is a set of constraints that makes alignment automatic and decisions cheaper. Its purpose is not tidiness; it is removing arbitrary choice.

THE PARAMETERS YOU MUST SPECIFY, per breakpoint:
- COLUMNS — the count. 12 is the web default because it divides by 2, 3, 4, and 6. 4 on mobile, 8 on tablet, 12 on desktop is the standard progression.
- GUTTER — the space between columns. Commonly 16–32px, from your spacing scale.
- MARGIN — the space outside the outermost columns. On mobile, 16–24px; on desktop, either a fixed value or a max-width container centred with auto margins.
- MAX CONTENT WIDTH — the cap beyond which the container stops growing. 1200–1440px for most product and marketing layouts; independent of the viewport width.

GRID TYPES AND WHEN EACH APPLIES:
- COLUMN GRID — the default for pages and marketing layouts.
- MODULAR GRID — columns plus rows, for dense card and dashboard layouts where vertical alignment matters as much as horizontal.
- BASELINE GRID — a fine vertical rhythm (typically 4 or 8px) that all type and spacing snaps to. Valuable in editorial and print-derived work, over-engineered for most product UI; the 8pt spacing scale delivers most of the benefit at a fraction of the cost.
- ASYMMETRIC GRID — deliberately unequal columns (e.g. 8+4 for content and sidebar). Strong, directional, and requires more decisions.
- BROKEN GRID — deliberate violation for emphasis. Only works if the grid is otherwise strictly held; breaking a grid nobody perceived communicates nothing.

WHAT THE GRID IS NOT FOR: text measure. A text block spanning eight columns on a 1440px screen is 800px wide and unreadable. The grid governs the container; the measure governs the text, independently.

IN FIGMA: set the layout grid on the frame, per breakpoint, as a saved grid style. Use grid layout mode or auto layout so the structure is enforced rather than eyeballed.

title: Measure, Rhythm, and Reading
content:
MEASURE — characters per line — is the most consequential and most neglected typographic setting in web layout.

THE NUMBERS: 45–75 characters per line for body text, 66 as the classic optimum, 35–50 for narrow columns and mobile. Over 75, the eye loses the return sweep and readers re-read lines. Under 40, the return is so frequent that rhythm breaks and hyphenation problems multiply.

HOW TO CONTROL IT: cap the text container, not the layout container. `max-width: 65ch` is the most direct expression; in Figma, set a max width on the text frame independent of its parent. A page can be 1440px wide with a 680px text column, and should be.

VERTICAL RHYTHM: consistent intervals let the reader predict where the next element will be, which is why a well-spaced page feels fast to scan even at the same information density.
- Establish a spacing scale (4/8-based) and use only its steps.
- Space by RELATIONSHIP, not by element: label→field 4–8px, field→field 16–24px, subsection→subsection 32–48px, section→section 64–128px.
- Keep the ratio between adjacent levels at 1.5× or more, or the difference is not perceptible and communicates nothing.

THE PROXIMITY RULE, which is the one that changes meaning: the gap WITHIN a group must be visibly smaller than the gap BETWEEN groups. Violating it makes elements appear to belong to the wrong thing. A heading closer to the paragraph above it than the one below it is attached to the wrong content, and readers follow the spacing, not the logic.

LINE HEIGHT SCALES INVERSELY WITH SIZE: body at 1.5–1.6, subheadings at 1.3–1.4, display at 1.1–1.25. A 48px headline at 1.5 line height floats apart; a 14px caption at 1.2 is cramped.

TRACKING: slightly negative on display sizes (−1% to −3%), zero on body, slightly positive on small caps and all-caps labels (+2% to +8%).

title: Whitespace — Active, Not Leftover
content:
Whitespace is a design material with three distinct jobs. Treating it as leftover space is what produces layouts that feel either cramped or arbitrary.

MICRO WHITESPACE — inside and immediately around elements. Padding, line height, letter spacing, gaps in a button. This governs LEGIBILITY. Its failures read as 'cramped' or 'sloppy'.

MACRO WHITESPACE — between sections and around major blocks. This governs STRUCTURE and PACE. Its failures read as 'busy' or 'disconnected'.

ACTIVE WHITESPACE — deliberate emptiness placed to isolate and emphasise. This governs FOCUS. A CTA with generous space around it reads as important without any change in size or colour. Isolation is the cheapest emphasis you can buy.

RULES:
- Whitespace is not wasted space. The argument 'we could fit more' is a request to reduce the value of everything already there, because attention is the constrained resource, not pixels.
- More whitespace reads as more premium and more considered; less reads as more urgent and more utilitarian. Both are valid — retail discount pages are deliberately dense, luxury pages deliberately sparse. Choose consciously.
- Whitespace must be consistent to be perceived as intentional. Three different section gaps read as an error; one repeated gap reads as a system.
- TRAPPED WHITESPACE is the failure mode: a gap inside a group larger than the gap around it, or an awkward void between two elements that belongs to neither. Fix by re-grouping, not by filling.
- Asymmetric whitespace creates direction and tension. Symmetric creates calm and stability. Both deliberate.

THE DENSITY DECISION IS A USER DECISION: professional tools used for hours need density, because scrolling and hidden context cost experts more than visual noise. Consumer products used briefly need air. Applying consumer airiness to a professional tool is one of the most common and most damaging layout errors.

title: Alignment and Optical Adjustment
content:
MECHANICAL alignment matches bounding boxes. OPTICAL alignment matches what the eye perceives. They differ, and the eye wins.

WHERE OPTICAL CORRECTION IS REQUIRED:
- ROUND AND POINTED SHAPES need to overshoot. A circle mechanically aligned with a square next to it looks smaller and higher; it must extend slightly past on all sides.
- ICONS WITH TEXT. Icon bounding boxes include padding that glyphs do not. An icon mechanically centred with a text baseline usually sits too high; nudge down 1px and check at 100%.
- UPPERCASE AND ALL-CAPS text in a button sits optically high because there are no descenders. Equal top and bottom padding looks bottom-heavy; reduce bottom padding slightly.
- PUNCTUATION AND QUOTES at the start of a line should hang outside the text block (hanging punctuation) so the text edge stays straight.
- CENTRED TEXT with a trailing punctuation mark or an icon appears off-centre. Centre the visual mass, not the box.

WHERE MECHANICAL ALIGNMENT IS NON-NEGOTIABLE:
- Left edges of stacked text blocks. Any variance reads as broken.
- Column edges across sections. Content that shifts 4px between two sections looks like a bug.
- Baselines of text sitting side by side.
- Right edges of numeric columns — right-align or decimal-align with tabular figures.

THE 9-POINT ALIGNMENT GRID: every element aligns to one of nine points relative to its container (three horizontal × three vertical). Being able to name which point an element uses is the difference between a system and improvisation.

RULE FOR OPTICAL WORK: make the correction, then document it. An undocumented optical nudge is indistinguishable from a mistake, and the next person will 'fix' it back to mechanical.

title: Responsive Strategy — Deciding How Layouts Change
content:
Reflow is a set of design decisions, not an automatic property. Undesigned reflow is engineering guessing at design.

FOR EVERY REGION, choose one behaviour as the width decreases:
- REFLOW — the same elements, rearranged. A 3-up card grid becomes 2-up then 1-up.
- STACK — side-by-side becomes vertical. Decide the ORDER, which is a content-priority decision, not a visual one.
- RESIZE — the element shrinks proportionally. Fine for images, dangerous for text and targets.
- SCROLL — the content overflows in one axis. Correct for tables and card rails; requires a visible affordance.
- DISCLOSE — the content collapses behind an accordion, tab, or drawer. Requires a decision about what the majority needs on every visit.
- TRANSFORM — the element becomes a different pattern entirely. A table becomes cards; a sidebar becomes a bottom sheet; a hover menu becomes a tap-to-expand.
- DROP — the content is removed. The weakest option: if it is unnecessary on mobile, question whether it is necessary at all.

CHOOSING BREAKPOINTS: derive them from where the CONTENT breaks, not from device names. Design the layout, widen and narrow it, and put a breakpoint where it stops working. Then reconcile with common device widths. Typical set: 0–599 (mobile), 600–904 (large mobile / small tablet), 905–1239 (tablet / small laptop), 1240+ (desktop).

WHAT IS ALWAYS SKIPPED: the 768–1024 range. Mobile and desktop get designed; the middle is interpolated and breaks. Design at least one middle width explicitly.

THE FOLD IS NOT WHERE FIGMA SAYS: browser chrome and dynamic mobile toolbars take 100–150px that a device frame does not model. Verify on a real device.

CONTENT-OUT, NOT CANVAS-IN: start from what each region needs (minimum readable measure, minimum legible image, minimum viable table) and let those minimums determine the layout, rather than dividing a canvas and hoping content fits.

title: Above the Fold — What It Is Actually For
content:
The fold is not a hard boundary — people scroll, and have since the 1990s. But the first viewport determines whether they scroll, which makes it the highest-leverage space on any page.

THE FIRST VIEWPORT MUST ANSWER THREE QUESTIONS in about three seconds:
1. WHAT IS THIS? A specific value proposition, not a slogan. 'Inventory management for Shopify brands doing over £1M' beats 'Grow faster'.
2. IS IT FOR ME? A signal of audience — the product shown in context, a named segment, a recognisable use case.
3. WHAT DO I DO NEXT? One unambiguous primary action.

WHAT WASTES IT, reliably:
- A full-viewport image with a two-word headline. Beautiful, and it answers none of the three questions.
- A carousel. Only the first slide gets meaningful engagement, so slides two onward are effectively unpublished — and the rotation actively costs comprehension.
- A cookie banner, a promo bar, an app-install prompt, and a newsletter modal occupying the first viewport in combination.
- Entrance animation on the hero, which delays comprehension and hurts LCP.
- Navigation and chrome taking a third of the height.
- A headline that describes the company rather than the user's outcome.

WHAT EARNS IT:
- Specific headline, one supporting sentence, one primary CTA, one secondary path for the not-yet-ready.
- Evidence in the first viewport — a real product screenshot, a number, a named customer. Product-in-context outperforms abstract illustration on almost every measure.
- A visible reason to scroll: a partially visible next section, so the page does not appear to end.

MOBILE SPECIFICALLY: the first viewport is roughly 375×550 of usable space after chrome. That is a headline, a line of support, and a button. Everything else is a scroll decision, so make the scroll decision easy.

title: Section Rhythm — Structuring a Long Page
content:
A long page is a sequence, and sequences need pacing. Most bad long pages are a stack of unrelated blocks at identical intervals.

THE MECHANICS:
- SECTION SPACING SCALE. Pick two or three values (e.g. 64 / 96 / 128) and use gap size to encode relatedness: closely related sections get the small gap, topic changes get the large one. Uniform section gaps discard this channel entirely.
- ALTERNATING STRUCTURE. Vary the layout between sections — full-width, then two-column, then centred narrow, then a grid. Identical structure repeated is what makes a page feel long.
- BACKGROUND CHANGES as chapter markers. A surface colour change is the strongest section boundary available and should be used sparingly, for genuine chapters, not every block.
- WIDTH VARIATION. Narrow for prose, wide for grids and imagery. Constant width reads as monotonous and forces bad measure on the text.
- ONE IDEA PER SECTION. If a section needs two headings of equal weight, it is two sections.

THE PACING PATTERN THAT WORKS for marketing and landing pages:
Hook (what and for whom) → Proof (evidence it works) → Mechanism (how it works) → Depth (details for the interested) → Objection handling (pricing, FAQ, comparison) → Close (the CTA again, with the reason restated).
Repeat the primary CTA at each natural decision point, roughly every two to three sections. Readers who are convinced early should not have to scroll to the bottom.

WHAT TO CHECK:
- Scroll the whole page fast. Does it feel like a sequence with a shape, or a list?
- Cover the copy. Can you still tell where sections begin and end?
- Count the section gap values in use. More than three is arbitrariness; exactly one is a missed channel.

title: Page Archetype — Landing and Marketing Page
content:
ANATOMY, in order:
1. Navigation — minimal. Logo, three to five links, one CTA. A marketing nav with twelve items is an org chart.
2. Hero — the three questions (ly-007), one primary CTA, one secondary.
3. Social proof strip — logos, a number, or a rating. Immediately after the hero, because the hero's claim needs corroboration before the reader invests in scrolling.
4. Problem or outcome section — the reader's situation named in their words.
5. Mechanism — how it works, ideally in three steps with a visual per step.
6. Feature depth — grouped by user benefit, not by system module.
7. Detailed proof — a case study, a metric, a quote with a name and a face.
8. Objection handling — pricing, comparison, FAQ, security, integration.
9. Final CTA — restating the value, not just the button.
10. Footer — the actual navigation, including everything the nav omitted.

PITFALLS:
- Feature list organised by your codebase. Users do not care about your modules.
- Testimonials without names, roles, or faces. Anonymous praise reads as invented.
- Three CTAs of equal weight in the hero.
- A pricing section with no prices.
- An FAQ that answers questions nobody asked while omitting the real objection.
- Nav CTA and hero CTA with different labels, so the reader cannot tell if they are the same action.
- Illustration where a screenshot belongs. Showing the actual product outperforms abstraction for anything with a demonstrable interface.

MEASUREMENT: scroll depth per section tells you where you lose people; CTA click-through per position tells you where the decision is actually made. Both are cheap to instrument and settle most layout arguments about this page type.

title: Page Archetype — Product Detail Page
content:
ANATOMY:
- MEDIA — the largest element. Multiple angles, scale reference, zoom, and video where relevant. Media quality is the strongest single conversion factor on this page type.
- TITLE, PRICE, AVAILABILITY — immediately adjacent, above the fold, unambiguous.
- VARIANT SELECTORS — swatches for colour, buttons for size. Never a dropdown for fewer than about seven options. Unavailable combinations must be visibly unavailable BEFORE selection.
- QUANTITY AND ADD TO CART — one dominant, filled, persistent action. On mobile, a sticky bottom bar carrying price and the CTA.
- SHIPPING AND RETURNS — near the price, not in the footer. This is where the abandonment decision is made.
- SHORT DESCRIPTION — the reason to buy, in three lines.
- TRUST SIGNALS — reviews summary near the price, full reviews further down, payment marks near the CTA.
- SPECIFICATIONS — accordion or tabs. Dimensions, materials, compatibility, care.
- FULL REVIEWS — with photos, filters, and the distribution, not just the average.
- RELATED AND COMPLEMENTARY — 'complete the look' outperforms 'similar items' for basket value; 'similar' matters when the shopper is still deciding.

PITFALLS:
- Price discoverable only after variant selection, with no starting price.
- Add to cart with no visible confirmation. The most expensive small omission in commerce.
- Sizing information behind a modal with no size guidance inline.
- Variant selection that reloads the page and loses scroll.
- Review average without count or distribution — 4.5 from three reviews is not 4.5 from three thousand.
- Cross-sells above the buy box.

SHOPIFY NOTES: check that the theme's variant selector reflects real inventory, that media loads without layout shift (a Core Web Vitals and conversion issue), and that the sticky mobile buy bar does not obscure content. See shopify-lore for platform mechanics.

title: Page Archetype — Collection, Search, and Results
content:
ANATOMY:
- CONTEXT HEADER — what this collection is, how many items, and why it exists. A bare grid with no context orphans the visitor arriving from search.
- SORT AND FILTER — sort as a compact control, filters as a sidebar on desktop and a bottom sheet on mobile. Show the applied filters as removable chips above the grid.
- RESULT COUNT — always. It tells the shopper whether to filter further or start browsing.
- THE GRID — 2-up mobile, 3–4 tablet, 4–6 desktop. Card contents: image, title, price, one differentiator, and an availability signal.
- PAGINATION OR LOAD MORE — 'Load more' beats infinite scroll for anything the user might want to leave and return to, because infinite scroll destroys the back button and the footer.
- ZERO RESULTS — the state that matters most and is designed least. It must say what was searched, why nothing matched, and offer a path: relax a filter, a spelling suggestion, or popular alternatives.

PITFALLS:
- Filtering that jumps the user to the top of the page. Preserve scroll, or design the loading state honestly.
- Filters that cannot be removed without opening the panel again.
- No indication of which filters are applied after the panel closes.
- Cards with inconsistent image treatment — mixed backgrounds, mixed crops, mixed aspect ratios. This is the most visible quality signal in a grid.
- Hover-only quick-view as the only path to detail.
- Sort options that do not persist.
- A grid that looks broken with one result. Design the minimum case.

LAYOUT CRAFT: card aspect ratio and image treatment matter more than card styling. Fix the aspect ratio, standardise the background, and align the text baselines across the row so titles of different lengths do not create a ragged grid — this usually means a fixed-height title area with truncation at two lines.

title: Page Archetype — Dashboard and Data View
content:
ANATOMY, by priority:
- THE ANSWER FIRST. The top of a dashboard should state the conclusion, not present raw material. 'Revenue is up 12% on last month' or a small set of KPI tiles with a comparison baseline. A dashboard that opens with a chart requiring interpretation has offloaded its job.
- COMPARISON BASELINE on every number. A figure without a previous period, target, or benchmark is uninterpretable.
- TIME RANGE CONTROL, global, obvious, and persistent across navigation.
- PRIMARY VISUALISATION — one chart that carries the main story, sized to dominate.
- SUPPORTING BREAKDOWNS — by segment, channel, or category, smaller.
- DETAIL TABLE — the raw rows, at the bottom, with sort, filter, and export.
- ALERTS AND ANOMALIES — surfaced, not buried. If something needs attention, it should not require the user to notice it.

LAYOUT PRINCIPLES SPECIFIC TO DATA VIEWS:
- Density is correct here. Professional users lose more from scrolling and hidden context than from visual busyness. Do not apply consumer airiness.
- Fuse the data (Gerhardt-Powals). Show 'available to spend', not balance + pending + reserved for the user to subtract.
- Align numbers right or on the decimal, with tabular figures. Left-aligned numeric columns cannot be scanned.
- One chart type per comparison type, consistently. Switching between bar and line for the same kind of comparison forces re-learning.
- Never animate a value that a user might be reading.
- Empty and low-data states are the first thing every new user sees. A dashboard designed only for the account with two years of history fails at onboarding.

PITFALLS: KPI tiles with no baseline; dual y-axes; pie charts with more than five slices; truncated y-axes on bar charts; filters that reset on navigation; a chart with no way to see the underlying rows.

title: Page Archetype — Forms and Multi-Step Flows
content:
LAYOUT RULES:
- ONE COLUMN. Multi-column forms cause skipped fields and ambiguous tab order. The exception is genuinely paired data (city/postcode, expiry/CVC) on one row.
- LABELS ABOVE FIELDS, always visible. Placeholder-as-label fails the moment the user types, and fails screen readers entirely. Left-aligned labels beside fields cost horizontal space and scan worse.
- GROUP BY MEANING with spacing, and use the proximity rule strictly: label→field tight, field→field medium, group→group large.
- FIELD WIDTH SIGNALS EXPECTED LENGTH. A postcode field the width of an email field is a small lie the user notices.
- ERRORS INLINE, adjacent to the field, in text as well as colour, validated on blur rather than on keystroke.
- ONE PRIMARY ACTION at the end, with secondary actions visually subordinate and destructive actions separated.
- OPTIONAL VS REQUIRED: mark the minority. If most fields are required, mark the optional ones.

MULTI-STEP FLOWS:
- Progress indication on anything over two steps, showing position and total.
- Group by the user's mental model, not the database. 'About you', 'Your delivery', 'Payment' — not 'users table', 'addresses table'.
- Back must preserve entered data. Losing input on back is the single most enraging form failure.
- Review before submit for anything consequential, showing everything entered with an edit link per section.
- Save-and-resume for anything long, and say that it exists before the user commits.

WHAT TO CHALLENGE BEFORE LAYING OUT ANYTHING: the field count. Every field costs completion rate. For each one, ask what breaks if it is not collected now. Deferring fields to post-signup is usually the highest-value change available on this page type, and it is a layout decision only after it is a scope decision.

title: Page Archetype — Application Shell and Navigation
content:
THE SHELL is the frame everything else lives in, and its cost is paid on every screen. Chrome that takes 30% of the viewport takes 30% of every task.

PATTERNS AND WHEN EACH FITS:
- TOP NAV — few sections, content-led products, marketing-adjacent apps. Cheapest vertically on wide screens, worst for many destinations.
- SIDEBAR — many destinations, deep hierarchy, professional tools. Collapsible to icons for density. Costs horizontal space, which is the cheaper axis on desktop.
- SIDEBAR + TOP BAR — the standard for complex products: sidebar for destinations, top bar for context, search, and account.
- BOTTOM TAB BAR — mobile, three to five top-level destinations, thumb-reachable. The correct mobile pattern for anything used frequently.
- HAMBURGER — mobile with many destinations, or secondary navigation. It halves discoverability of what it hides; acceptable for the long tail, wrong for primary destinations.
- COMMAND PALETTE — expert accelerator, never the only path.

RULES:
- Show current location unambiguously. An active state that is a slightly different grey is not a state.
- Keep primary destinations to a number a user can hold — five to seven. Beyond that, group, and be explicit about the grouping logic.
- Collapse chrome on scroll rather than pinning everything. A header, sub-header, breadcrumb, and toolbar all pinned leaves a viewport for the content.
- Search is a navigation pattern once you have more than a few dozen destinations. Treat it as primary, not as an icon.
- The logo links home. Always. This is external consistency and violating it costs you nothing to fix.
- Settings, account, and help are the long tail; they belong in a menu, not the primary nav.

MOBILE PARITY: every task must be completable on a phone. A sidebar that becomes a hamburger, hiding the only path to the primary task, is a shell failure disguised as a responsive decision.

title: Layout Anti-Patterns
content:
THE PINTEREST TRAP. A layout copied from a visual reference and filled with your content. The reference was designed for its content; yours is different. Symptom: it breaks the first time real data arrives.

CARD SOUP. Everything in a card because a card component existed. Cards imply peer-level, self-contained, individually actionable items. A card around a paragraph of prose communicates nothing and adds two borders and 32px of padding.

THE EQUAL-WEIGHT GRID. Six features in six identical boxes, so the layout asserts they are equally important. They are not. Rank them and show the ranking.

CENTRED EVERYTHING. Centred multi-line text has no consistent left edge, so scanning cost rises per line. Centre headlines and short labels only.

FULL-WIDTH TEXT. Body copy spanning a 1440px viewport. Cap the measure independently of the container.

THE CAROUSEL. Only the first slide gets meaningful engagement. If content matters, it should not be behind a rotation the user must wait for; if it does not matter, remove it.

CHROME EXCEEDING CONTENT. Header, sub-header, breadcrumb, toolbar, and filter bar with a third of the viewport left for the actual thing.

ACCORDION EVERYTHING. Collapsing content that most users need on every visit, taxing the majority to tidy up for a minority.

FIXED HEIGHTS. Any fixed-height container meeting variable content will eventually clip. Design from minimum height plus growth.

DESKTOP-FIRST WITH 'IT'LL REFLOW'. Reflow is a set of decisions. Undesigned reflow is engineering designing.

DECORATION IN THE PRIMARY POSITION. A hero image occupying the space where the value proposition and the action should be.

IDEAL-DATA-ONLY LAYOUT. Designed with three items of similar length. Production has zero, one, or four hundred, with one title nine words long.

SYMMETRY BY DEFAULT. Two equal columns because the canvas divided evenly, with no relationship between the content in them.

title: Designing Layouts That Survive Implementation
content:
A layout is a set of instructions. Ambiguity is filled in by whoever builds it.

WHAT MAKES A LAYOUT BUILDABLE AS DESIGNED:
- AUTO LAYOUT EVERYWHERE. It encodes the intent — what hugs, what fills, what has a fixed size, how gaps behave — rather than leaving positions to be inferred from coordinates. A layout built with absolute positioning is a screenshot.
- SIZING BEHAVIOUR STATED per element: fill, hug, fixed, with min and max where relevant. This maps directly to flex and grid properties.
- EVERY SPACING VALUE FROM A TOKEN. Hardcoded spacing becomes a hardcoded value in code, which becomes drift.
- GRID SPECIFIED PER BREAKPOINT — columns, gutter, margin, max width. Put it in the file as a layout grid, not in a comment.
- MEASURE CAPS STATED as a value, because they will not be inferred.
- REFLOW BEHAVIOUR STATED per region (ly-006). Which stacks, in what order, at what width.
- OVERFLOW BEHAVIOUR STATED. What truncates, at how many lines, with what indicator. What wraps. What scrolls.
- THE STATES, because a layout with only its ideal state will have its other states invented.

WHAT TO SPECIFY THAT FIGMA CANNOT SHOW:
- Which gaps are fixed and which are proportional.
- Whether a two-column split is 50/50, 60/40, or content-driven.
- Whether an image is object-fit cover or contain, and its focal point.
- Line-clamp values.
- Whether a sticky element sticks to the viewport or to a container.

THE HANDOFF TEST: give the file to an engineer and ask them to state the grid, the reflow order, and the truncation rules from the file alone. Whatever they cannot answer is what you have left to chance — and it is where the build will differ from the design.

SHOPIFY SPECIFIC: layout regions map to sections and blocks, and merchant-configurable settings mean your layout must survive a merchant reordering it or leaving a field empty. Design for the settings schema, not just the one arrangement. See shopify-lore for the mapping.
